title: The AI Disclosure Paradox: The Uneven Signaling Effects of Providers' Disclosure of AI Adoption
affiliations: Tel Aviv University - Coller School of Management and Tel Aviv University - Coller School of Management

detail.title: The AI Disclosure Paradox: The Uneven Signaling Effects of Providers' Disclosure of AI Adoption

declarations.ethicsApproval: This research was approved by the Tel Aviv University Institutional Review Board.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program (#759540), awarded to Prof. Gal Oestreicher-Singer.

detail.abstract: With the growing adoption of AI, industry leaders and policymakers are working to establish best practices and regulations for the disclosure of AI adoption. While recent research has examined how consumers perceive AI-generated products, we focus on the role of AI adoption disclosure as a signal when choosing service providers. Particularly, to isolate the signal embedded in the adoption itself, we study AI pricing adoption, which does not directly affect service quality. In a series of studies conducted on a simulated gig-economy platform, we find that disclosing AI pricing adoption negatively affects consumer demand. Exploring the mechanism behind this adverse effect suggests that consumers perceive AI adopters as less professional and less trustworthy than service providers who do not use AI, a phenomenon we refer to as "AI-adopter aversion." Surprisingly, we also show that the majority of consumers perceive AI pricing to be more beneficial to them compared with human-generated pricing. We explain these seemingly paradoxical findings by showing that the impact on consumers who perceive AI adoption negatively is significantly negative, while the impact on consumers who perceive it positively is insignificant. Our findings expand current theoretical understanding of AI aversion, providing significant implications for AI policy and regulation.

title: The Embedded Game: Incentive Mechanics and Structural Consequences
affiliations: La Trobe University

detail.title: The Embedded Game: Incentive Mechanics and Structural Consequences
detail.abstract: Game theory provides formal models of strategic interaction, explaining how rational agents respond to incentives under conditions of interdependence. While traditionally applied to discrete markets, negotiations, and political competition, these models also illuminate the structural dynamics of everyday social participation. Modern social systems operate as persistent, overlapping strategic environments in which participation is structurally compulsory, incentives are actively engineered, time horizons are compressed, and early positioning constrains future mobility. Drawing on canonical game-theoretic models-including repeated games, signalling games, public goods frameworks, sequential equilibria, and multi-sided market theory-this paper formalises seven structural rules governing embedded participation. By integrating insights from behavioural economics and systems theory, the analysis links micro-level decision mechanics to broader structural consequences across domains such as politics, education, debt, and platform economies. The result is a disciplined micro-foundational framework that clarifies how incentive architectures shape strategic positioning without invoking macro-level collapse dynamics.

detail.abstract: We compare physician incomes using tax data from the United States, Canada, Sweden, and the Netherlands. Physicians are concentrated in the top percentiles of the income distribution in all four countries, especially in the United States and certain specialties. Physician incomes are highest in the United States, and a decomposition shows that this mainly reflects differences in overall income distributions, rather than physicians' locations in those distributions. This suggests that broader labor market differences, and thus physicians' outside options, drive absolute incomes. Shifting US physicians' incomes to match relative positions in other countries' distributions would only marginally reduce healthcare spending.

title: Free Isn't Cheap: Zero Pricing Protects Luxury Brands in Blockchain-Based Digital Collectible Extensions

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP24K16464 and 25K00676

detail.abstract: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) present luxury brands with a pricing dilemma: high prices sustain quality inferences but invite visible failure on transparent blockchain markets, whereas low prices stimulate demand but anchor perceptions downward. This research investigates zero pricing (free distribution) as a strategy to navigate this dilemma. Analysis of 65 NFT collections from 32 brands on OpenSea and 22,841 posts on X is followed by six experiments (N = 1,924). Low-priced NFTs inflict the most severe loss of brand luxuriousness, yet free NFTs attenuate this loss to levels indistinguishable from comparable pricing (Study 1). This attenuation does not extend to physical products, implicating congruence between inferred cost structure and zero pricing as a governing condition (Study 2). When secondary-market demand declines, free NFTs weaken failure inferences that otherwise erode perceived luxury; however, this buffer dissipates when the NFT features flagship brand elements (Studies 3a-3c). When demand increases, free and paid NFTs yield equivalent recovery (Study 4). Free distribution thus caps downside risk without forfeiting upside potential. These findings advance the zero-price literature by establishing inferred cost structure as a boundary condition for the anchor-shift mechanism and equip brand managers with a pricing approach calibrated to the transparency of blockchain-based markets.

title: Merit: A multi-objective basket currency index for neutral global settlement

detail.title: Merit: A multi-objective basket currency index for neutral global settlement
detail.abstract: I propose Merit, a synthetic global currency index designed for neutral cross-border settlement. The index is constructed from the currencies of the 20 largest economies by GDP, consolidated into 16 currency zones, with weights determined by a six-objective optimiser that jointly minimises variance, downside risk, conditional tail risk, historical stress loss, turnover, and GDP-anchor deviation, subject to an adaptive concentration cap and a USD-bloc constraint. A monthly backtest over 2000-2025 using the Swiss franc as numeraire yields 5.51% annualised volatility (stability ratio 0.59), lower than 15 of 16 constituents. Sensitivity analysis indicates robustness to parameter choice: varying each penalty multiplier across its full range changes volatility by at most 3 basis points, with the adaptive cap coefficient k as the sole materially influential parameter (36 basis points). Benchmark comparisons against the IMF SDR, equal-weight, minimum-variance, and GDP-proportional baskets suggest a favourable joint trade-off across volatility, tail risk (kurtosis 4.02 versus 8.60 for the unconstrained minimum-variance basket), and concentration. A formal adoption utility function incorporating network externalities, transaction cost savings, and sanction-risk hedging characterises the critical-mass threshold for self-sustaining adoption. A six-layer permissioned settlement architecture targets 2.5-second deterministic finality at 12,000 transactions per second, governed by a tri-chamber institutional structure with hard parameter bounds. A cost model calibrated from BIS, World Bank, and McKinsey data estimates 79% median savings over SWIFT correspondent banking. The paper analyses the political economy of adoption under dollar dominance, sanctions regimes, and central bank resistance, identifying three adoption pathways ordered by political difficulty, and systematically assesses risks including basket instability, liquidity fragmentation, governance capture, speculative attacks, and regulatory suppression.

title: From Universal Basic Income to Minimum Sovereign Production Units (MSPUs): Productive Autonomy and Power Asymmetry in the Age of Physical Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: As AI and robotics displace human labor, Universal Basic Income (UBI) is widely proposed to preserve welfare under technological unemployment. This paper argues that redistribution alone is structurally insufficient when citizens are fully alienated from embodied productive capacity. In digitized welfare regimes, income becomes an administratively mediated permission system-centrally authorized, conditionally continuous, and instantly reversible-creating a new asymmetry of power under full automation. We propose Minimum Sovereign Production Units (MSPUs) as a capability-based autonomy baseline: individually owned, physically embodied cyber-physical systems that provide a legally protected floor of productive autonomy, including offline continuity for essential functions. Unlike income transfers, embodied productive capability cannot be nullified at low administrative cost through purely digital revocation without overt coercion, shifting autonomy from administrative permission to material capability. We outline regulatory approaches to corporate concentration of physical agency via caps on control rights over robotic capacity, alongside constrained certification regimes that govern operation rather than ownership. We conclude that embedding productive autonomy into standards and law during the current transitional window is necessary to prevent future redistributive systems from devolving into managed subsistence rather than emancipatory welfare.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a conceptual framework for explaining the sustained high fertility of religious communities under conditions of generalized demographic crisis. Despite an extensive literature documenting the correlation between religiosity and fertility, existing explanations suffer from categorical underdifferentiation and fail to integrate ideational and structural approaches into a unified analytical model. This article addresses that gap by introducing the concept of solidarity infrastructure-an ensemble of institutionalized mechanisms that simultaneously reduce the marginal costs of reproduction and raise its normative value. The infrastructure is operationalized through six mechanisms: mutual aid and collective childcare (M1), alternative economic architecture (M2), narrative infrastructure of meaning (M3), intergenerational norm transmission (M4), endogamous marriage market control (M5), and residential concentration (M6). Employing a Most Different Systems Design strategy, the article compares Ultra-Orthodox Jews, the Amish, Israeli kibbutzim, and post-revolutionary Iran. The central argument is formulated asymmetrically: normative pronatalism without enabling infrastructure is demographically ineffective-a thesis corroborated by the Iranian paradox and the kibbutz quasi-experiment. The analysis yields six testable hypotheses for subsequent empirical research.

title: Long-Term Blockade of the Strait of Hormuz: A Scenario Analysis of Global Macroeconomic Crisis and Institutional Response Guidelines
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Long-Term Blockade of the Strait of Hormuz: A Scenario Analysis of Global Macroeconomic Crisis and Institutional Response Guidelines
detail.abstract: The Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint handling nearly 30% of seaborne oil trade, faces severe risks from longterm blockade (over 30 days). This paper simulates the crisis transmission chain triggered by a daily 10-15 million barrel oil supply gap: irreversible oilfield shutdowns, strategic reserve exhaustion in 55 days, full-blown stagflation, monetary policy failure under a 300% global debt-to-GDP ratio, emerging market collapse, and a deep global depression. It identifies Day 30 as the irreversible crisis threshold and Day 55 as the global financial system's viability line, comparing this crisis's severity to the 1973 oil crisis and 2008 financial crisis. Targeted, actionable response strategies are proposed for central banks, financial institutions, asset managers, and investors, providing a critical reference for institutional decision-makers to assess and mitigate geopolitical and energy-driven systemic risks.

title: ABVIE: A Deterministic Architecture for Reliable AI-Driven Financial Analysis

detail.title: ABVIE: A Deterministic Architecture for Reliable AI-Driven Financial Analysis
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to financial analytics, reporting, and decision-support systems. However, their probabilistic nature often produces numerical hallucinations, plausible but mathematically incorrect outputs that undermine reliability in financial environments where accuracy is critical. This paper introduces ABVIE (Automated Business Valuation & Intelligence Engine), a deterministic financial intelligence architecture designed to eliminate numerical hallucinations by separating financial computation from language model interpretation. The proposed architecture implements a Math Firewall that ensures all financial calculations are executed exclusively by deterministic computational engines while generative models are restricted to narrative explanation. Computation outputs are stored within an immutable Fact Store and verified through a numeric reconciliation mechanism that prevents unverified numerical outputs. Preliminary evaluation comparing ABVIE with a baseline GPT-4 powered financial analysis agent demonstrates that the architecture eliminates numerical hallucinations while maintaining interpretive capabilities. The proposed framework provides a viable architectural approach for building trustworthy AI-driven financial intelligence systems suitable for institutional financial environments.

title: Crypto-Native Fixed Income: Duration and Convexity by Construction on the EVM

detail.title: Crypto-Native Fixed Income: Duration and Convexity by Construction on the EVM
detail.abstract:
Decentralized finance has built fixed-rate and yield-bearing instruments, but not a fixed-income architecture in which duration and convexity arise endogenously from continuously updated collateral-policy logic. Every existing protocol that expresses rate sensitivity either imports it from a traditional financial asset, derives it from an automated market maker price curve, or constructs it as a synthetic derivative position. None generate rate sensitivity endogenously from on-chain collateral architecture. This paper shows that a deterministic collateral release schedule defined on a state-aware policy surface is sufficient to endow an on-chain debt instrument with computable modified duration and asymmetric rate sensitivity by construction.

We introduce the Amortizing Collateral Bond (ACB), a crypto-native debt instrument whose financial characteristics emerge from collateral policy architecture rather than from any imported traditional finance instrument. The ACB's modified duration is derived analytically from its release schedule and a protocol-implied discount rate. Asymmetric rate sensitivity—the property that the instrument loses more from rate rises than it gains from rate declines, analogous to the convexity profile of a mortgage-backed security holder—arises from two state-machine-enforced mechanisms: a prepayment option that compresses price appreciation when rates fall, and regime-dependent release schedules that extend duration when rates rise. Neither requires a counterparty or clearing house to enforce the option schedule. We further introduce the Prepayable Vault with Embedded Callable Option, which makes the convexity compression explicit and parameterizable, and Duration-Tranched Vault Certificates, which generalize the structure to multi-tranche pools tranched by rate sensitivity rather than credit quality.

In Stage 2, we generalize the discount rate from a protocol-implied single rate to a composite on-chain rate index constructed from observable lending, staking, and funding markets—enabling multi-maturity duration computation and an empirical low-correlation claim against the Treasury curve. We show that this composite index admits a term structure adequate for duration analysis across maturities, and argue that its structural drivers are distinct from those of the Treasury yield curve—not as a portfolio-level diversification claim, but as a property of the rate surface itself. The empirical correlation between the two surfaces is low over the 2022–2024 period; we are explicit that this independence is structural rather than permanent, and that it degrades as institutional capital integrates the two surfaces. We engage directly with the market-readiness constraints—rate surface liquidity, hedging ecosystem development, and the adoption sequencing problem—and frame the contribution honestly as a proof of existence for crypto-native fixed income rather than a complete market design.

The paper further introduces the Collateralized Amortizing Obligation (CAO)—a crypto-native structured vehicle with duration-stratified Senior, Mezzanine, and Equity tranches enforced by a deterministic waterfall. The CAO is not a tokenized collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO) or collateralized loan obligation (CLO): its collateral is entirely on-chain, its tranche duration profiles are computable from the policy surface architecture, and its return drivers reference a rate surface with structurally distinct drivers from traditional finance (TradFi) rate markets. Full issuance mechanics, atomic settlement, and the Convexity Swap as the Equity tranche hedging instrument are developed in Paper III.

The architecture developed in Paper I is the necessary prerequisite. A well-defined, continuously updated policy surface is the precondition for any of these instruments to be constructible. What follows shows what becomes possible once that precondition is met.

title: The Material Limits of Utopia: A Soviet Teacher’s Diary as Evidence of Infrastructure Collapse, 1929–1936

detail.abstract: Drawing on an unpublished diary kept by Ilya Vasilievich Gudkov between 1929 and 1935 and cross-referenced with regional inspection reports, Workers’ and Peasants’ Inspection (RKI) audits, educational press, and pedological surveys, this article argues that personal tragedy in the Soviet school system can be read as evidence of systemic infrastructure collapse. The case of Gudkov and his family reveals the material limits of Soviet educational utopianism, where ideological ambition repeatedly collided with cold classrooms, absent medical care, and failing housing conditions. It further shows that pedology had already quantified the link between deprivation, illness, and school failure before its liquidation in July 1936 removed a key diagnostic instrument from Soviet education.

title: Deterministic Structured Credit for DeFi: Designing On-Chain Waterfalls, State Machines, and Duration-Aware Risk

detail.title: Deterministic Structured Credit for DeFi: Designing On-Chain Waterfalls, State Machines, and Duration-Aware Risk
detail.abstract:
Traditional asset managers are increasingly tokenizing structured credit portfolios, yet most tokenized instruments remain economically siloed. While shares may transfer on-chain, they cannot safely function as dynamic collateral within decentralized lending markets. The constraint is structural: static margin frameworks are poorly suited to amortizing credit assets whose duration, spread exposure, and liquidity evolve continuously. As interest rates rise and prepayments slow, effective duration extends while convexity becomes increasingly negative—increasing sensitivity to rate and spread shocks precisely when leverage remains fixed under static margin frameworks. This "Duration Gap" prevents structured credit from scaling as composable on-chain collateral—and closing it would allow institutional holders to access secured funding against credit positions without liquidating exposure. Early deployments—BlackRock's BUIDL accepted as collateral on major trading platforms, Ondo's OUSG integrated into decentralized finance (DeFi) lending protocols—demonstrate growing institutional demand for collateral-eligible real-world assets (RWAs), but existing static frameworks cannot accommodate instruments with regime-dependent duration and negative convexity.

This paper proposes a rule-based margin framework that closes the Duration Gap by functioning as an on-chain analogue to secured funding markets. A structured credit Risk Vector feeds a deterministic Credit State Machine, whose regime classifications drive smooth collateral policy surfaces that adjust margin parameters—collateral factors, haircuts, liquidation thresholds, and borrow caps—automatically as structural risk evolves. Rules are encoded directly into smart contracts, enabling automatic enforcement without discretionary governance or centralized risk committees. External lending protocols integrate without replicating the underlying credit model; they consume a standardized, programmatically broadcast margin feed.

Capital stack integrity is preserved through a Waterfall Engine segregating Senior and Equity exposure. Equity absorbs first-loss and mark-to-market volatility; Senior tokens receive priority cashflows and structural protection through immutable overcollateralization and amortization triggers. Margin policy and capital allocation remain orthogonal: leverage tightening does not alter tranche priority. The framework supports multi-tranche structures in which only senior exposures qualify as collateral primitives, mirroring repo desk eligibility standards.

Custody of underlying assets remains bankruptcy-remote and institutionally governed; risk discipline executes on-chain. External lending markets need not model convexity or amortization complexity—they query state-aware margin parameters broadcast programmatically. While validated on mortgage-backed securities (MBS), the architecture generalizes to any amortizing asset with observable risk metrics: collateralized loan obligation (CLO) tranches, private credit facilities, esoteric asset-backed securities (ABS), and other illiquid instruments currently absent from on-chain collateral markets. Monte Carlo stress validation across 1,000 correlated shock paths confirms bounded drawdowns, with 99.6% of paths recording zero emergency unwind days and no path exceeding two, and full Equity absorption of tail losses, leaving Senior holders unimpaired.

The resulting architecture allows tokenized credit instruments to function as programmable collateral primitives within decentralized lending systems while preserving the risk discipline of traditional capital markets—expanding tokenized assets from passive investment vehicles into active secured funding infrastructure whose value compounds with adoption: deeper liquidity improves collateral parameters, transparent margining compresses funding spreads, and greater issuance scale enriches the oracle infrastructure on which the framework depends.

title: To be or not to be a QSC? That is Another Question: Qualifying Sub-Contract Status under the Single Source Contract Regulations
affiliations: University of Nottingham

detail.title: To be or not to be a QSC? That is Another Question: Qualifying Sub-Contract Status under the Single Source Contract Regulations
detail.abstract: In 2014, the Ministry of Defence introduced the Defence Reform Act and Single Source Contract Regulations to regulate the pricing and oversight of single source defence contracts. This is supported by the establishment of the Single Source Regulations Office. The framework is complex and has undergone ad hoc reform over the years. A decade on, with the framework bedding down, now is an opportune moment to take stock of its development. As a logical starting point, it is useful to begin by considering coverage. A previous article examined coverage in respect of qualifying defence contracts ("QDCs"). This article examines qualifying sub-contracts ("QSCs"). Despite such contracts being a derivative of a prime QDC, these are subject to even more regulation and uncertainty. This raises questions about: the underlying policy objectives of the framework and procurement legislation more generally in respect of sub-contracting (e.g. in promoting competition and SMEs); whether the model governing assessments of sub-contracts is sufficiently tailored to a different commercial and contractual interface; legal and practical uncertainty in respect of various rules and policies; and the proportionality of regulation in this context. Reinforcing earlier arguments, the regime is too complex, too uncertain and has not been adequately addressed by piecemeal reforms. There is a need for more fundamental reform. Additional empirical research would help identify what is feasible in this regard.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the strategic logic behind the expansion of confrontation from a bilateral U.S.–Israel–Iran dynamic into a broader regional systemic crisis. Rather than interpreting escalation as reactive overreach, the study conceptualizes it as a structural recalibration of conflict architecture. Drawing on deterrence theory, asymmetric conflict research, strategic culture scholarship, and theories of systemic interdependence, the analysis argues that when confrontation is framed in existential terms, cost–benefit rationality shifts and escalation thresholds become fluid. The article demonstrates how expanding the theatre of conflict can redistribute strategic costs across regional alliances, energy corridors, industrial supply chains, and financial systems. Particular attention is given to the Gulf region as a structural vulnerability within the global energy order, where disruption carries disproportionate economic and geopolitical consequences. The study further explores asymmetric cost-exchange dynamics in modern warfare, highlighting how industrial sustainability and production depth increasingly shape long-term outcomes. By integrating insights from Surrender Theory, the paper contends that misreading cultural conceptions of endurance and legitimacy can generate strategic miscalculation. Historical parallels—from 1914 to 1973—illustrate how localized crises can evolve into systemic shocks when escalation intersects with global interdependence. The central argument is that contemporary escalation is less about battlefield dominance and more about control over systemic complexity. In an interconnected international order, the greatest danger lies not in initiating conflict, but in losing the ability to manage its cascading effects.

title: Exporting Automation, Not Just Goods: Evidence from China's Industrial Robot Exports
affiliations: , Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business and Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: Exporting Automation, Not Just Goods: Evidence from China's Industrial Robot Exports
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of who imports China's industrial robots, why they do so, and how competitive these robots are in global markets. Using bilateral trade data from 2005-2022, we document a structural transformation in China's position in global robotics trade: China has shifted from a net importer to a net exporter of industrial robots. Its exports are disproportionately directed toward emerging manufacturing hubs, particularly in Southeast Asia. Although Chinese robots are generally less technologically advanced than those produced by Japan, Germany, the United States, and South Korea, they offer the strongest "bang for the buck." These "good-enough" robots are especially attractive to price-sensitive, lower-income economies that are becoming new manufacturing platforms amid global supply-chain reconfiguration. Consistent with this mechanism, we document a U-shaped relationship between robot imports and GDP per capita: high-income economies adopt frontier robots to offset high labor costs, whereas low-income economies rely on cost-effective Chinese robots to compensate for weaker labor quality rather than high wages. Finally, using a fully specified general equilibrium framework, we conduct counterfactual policy simulations to evaluate how geopolitical and industrial policy shocks affect China's robot exports, relative wages, and global welfare. Our findings suggest that China is increasingly exporting production capability---not just products. More broadly, contrary to the view that automation substitutes for offshoring, our results show that cost-effective robots can travel with production as manufacturing relocates to lower-wage economies.

detail.abstract: Food security and environmentally friendly farming techniques are in dire need of creative solutions as the world's agricultural landscape faces previously unheard-of difficulties brought on by population increase, climate change, and changing consumer demands. This study looks at how ICT and AI in agriculture support sustainable development and food security in Nigeria. It examines how household food security and ICT/AI use are mediated by young employment, agricultural AI adoption, and farmers' ICT use. The study employed a survey research methodology. 300 urban farmers in the main Ebonyi State cities of Abakaliki, Afikpo, Onueke, Uburu, and Effium participated in a census approach to collect data. SWOT and PESTEL analyses were then utilized to give strategic insights. An 83.3 percent return rate was obtained from the 250 copies that were completed. The results show that while youth empowerment has a substantial impact on the association between food safety and ICT and IA, employing ICT and AI to provide access to markets, information, and support services considerably boosts household food security. It recommends the dissemination agents receive training in the usage of ICT platforms and AI technologies so they can provide farmers with accurate and timely advice.

title: “I Got You This Deal”: The Double-Edged Effects of Preferential Treatment Claims in Video Commerce
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Harbin Engineering University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Information Systems and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: “I Got You This Deal”: The Double-Edged Effects of Preferential Treatment Claims in Video Commerce
detail.abstract: In video commerce, influencers frequently claim that they have secured special discounts, extra gifts, or exclusive benefits for their followers. We conceptualize such preferential treatment claims as a transactional advocacy cue and examine their double-edged effects on consumer responses. Drawing on cue theory and persuasion knowledge theory, we propose that preferential treatment claims trigger two competing inferences: perceived altruism and skepticism. These inferences differentially shape purchase intention and comment intention, and their relative strength depends on influencer popularity. We test this framework across three studies: a large-scale analysis of more than 70,000 platform comments, a survey, and an experiment. Across studies, preferential treatment claims elicit both favorable and skeptical responses. Survey and experimental results show that these claims increase purchase intention indirectly through perceived altruism, while decreasing purchase intention and increasing comment intention through skepticism. The experiment further shows that influencer popularity shifts the inferential route through which preferential treatment claims operate: the advocacy pathway is stronger for lower-popularity influencers, whereas the skepticism pathway is stronger for higher-popularity influencers. This research contributes to the video commerce literature by identifying preferential treatment claims as a consequential transaction-related tactic, to influencer research by highlighting marketplace advocacy claims as a basis for follower-oriented judgments, and to cue theory by showing that a single cue can be both diagnostic and contestable in digital commerce environments.

title: Pricing Power vs. Fan Conversion: Channel Strategy in Platform Live Streaming
affiliations: Changzhou University, Changzhou University and Nanjing University

detail.title: Pricing Power vs. Fan Conversion: Channel Strategy in Platform Live Streaming

keywords.keywords: Live streaming \sep Fan conversion effect   \sep  Influencer \sep Channel strategy

detail.abstract: Live streaming commerce has emerged as a dominant channel in platform-based retail, raising a fundamental question: how should platforms and manufacturers jointly design channel structures and selling modes in the presence of influencer-driven demand? We develop a game-theoretic model that integrates live-streaming channel choices (self-operated vs. influencer-driven) with selling modes (agency vs. reselling), while explicitly capturing the influencer’s fan conversion effect.Our analysis reveals a key counterintuitive insight: pricing authority does not always benefit platforms. Even when platforms relinquish retail pricing control under the agency mode, overall performance can outperform that under the reselling structure. We further show that the agency–influencer configuration leads to lower retail prices and higher consumer surplus, whereas the reselling–influencer configuration induces stronger influencer effort. The optimal channel–mode combination is jointly shaped by live-streaming costs and commission rates.To enhance robustness, we extend the model by endogenizing commission rates via Nash bargaining. The main insights remain unchanged: stronger manufacturer bargaining power drives a shift toward agency modes, while higher live-streaming costs consistently favor influencer-driven channels.These findings provide actionable insights for platforms and manufacturers in configuring live-streaming channels and allocating pricing authority under influencer-driven market environments.

detail.title: Understanding millennial consumers’ adoption of remanufactured laptops in Indonesia: Implications for circular economy and biosustainability
detail.abstract: The increasing demand for laptops in Indonesia, particularly among millennial consumers, has raised significant environmental concerns due to the growing volume of electronic waste. Remanufacturing offers a sustainable solution by extending product lifecycles, conserving material resources, and reducing the ecological impact of electronic disposal. Despite these advantages, adoption of remanufactured laptops remains limited in Indonesia due to information asymmetry, perceived quality issues, and low consumer trust. This study adopts a mixed-methods approach, integrating a systematic literature review, MaxDiff choice-based conjoint analysis, Latent Class Analysis (LCA), and Total Unduplicated Reach and Frequency (TURF) simulation to identify and evaluate key indicators influencing the switching intentions of millennial consumers toward remanufactured laptops. The findings reveal three distinct consumer segments, Quality Enthusiasts, Practical Buyers, and Risk Assessors, each representing varying degrees of behavioral maturity and openness to remanufactured technology. Among the fourteen indicators examined, quality control procedures, price comparisons, and product condition upon return emerged as the most influential factors, collectively achieving an 82.67% weighted reach across segments. These insights highlight the critical need for targeted marketing strategies, transparent product communication, and educational interventions to bridge knowledge gaps and foster trust in remanufactured electronics. Emphasizing alignment with circular economy principles and biosustainability objectives, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of consumer behavior in developing markets and provides actionable insights for marketers, policymakers, and industry stakeholders to advance sustainable consumption and adoption of remanufactured electronics.

title: An AI-Powered Framework For Professional Credibility Verification A Multi-Service Platform for Evidence-Based Professional Identity at Scale

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces VERITA — a comprehensive AI-powered platform for professional credibility verification. It addresses a structural deficit at the heart of the global economy: professionals, organisations, and institutions routinely cannot prove what they can document. They can only state what they claim. The gap between claimed credibility and evidence-based credibility is the market failure VERITA is designed to close.

VERITA operationalises evidence-based credibility as a practical service architecture. The platform includes 35 active services spanning individual professional verification, academic document analysis, enterprise credential checking, insurance and compliance review, creator authority documentation, and blockchain certificate issuance. It operates natively in English, French, and Spanish. It is AI-agnostic, compatible with Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and open-source models.

The paper establishes evidence-based credibility as a distinct and measurable concept; describes VERITA’s four architectural principles, service taxonomy, and enterprise market applications across twelve sectors; presents the blockchain integration roadmap including the self-sovereign identity model; and positions VERITA against LinkedIn, Turnitin, Google, and established background-check providers. The competitive moat is precise: no existing platform combines document-based evidence reading, credibility scoring, professional document generation, multilingual operation, enterprise verification, and blockchain certificate issuance in a single system.

This working paper simultaneously constitutes a statement of prior authorship. It documents that Jean Claude Havyarimana conceived, designed, and built VERITA — its concept, architecture, services, enterprise vision, and blockchain roadmap — with first public deployment in March 2026.

title: Customer Experience as the Organism in Livestreaming Fashion Commerce: A Stimulus–Organism–Response Perspective​

detail.title: Customer Experience as the Organism in Livestreaming Fashion Commerce: A Stimulus–Organism–Response Perspective​
detail.abstract: Livestreaming has become a core format in electronic commerce, where social interaction, real time media, and promotional timing jointly shape consumer responses. Although prior studies have examined individual social and technical mechanisms in livestream commerce, less is known about how consumers form a holistic customer experience (CX) that translates livestream stimuli into behavioural and relational outcomes. Grounded in the Stimulus-Organism-Response framework, this study conceptualises CX as a second order organismic state that integrates cognitive, affective, social, and sensory appraisals in fashion livestreaming.Survey data from 374 fashion livestream shoppers in China were analysed using PLS-SEM to examine how parasocial interaction, interactivity, media richness, price benefit, and ease of use shape CX, and how CX subsequently influences trust, continuance intention, swift guanxi, herd behaviour, and the urge to buy impulsively. The results show that parasocial interaction is the strongest driver of CX, followed by price benefit, interactivity, and media richness. Ease of use is not significant, indicating that in high engagement, presenter led livestream formats, social and value-based cues outweigh marginal technical usability. CX positively predicts all five outcomes and serves as a key mediating mechanism, transmitting the effects of significant stimuli to behavioural and relational responses. The findings position multidimensional CX as the central psychological mechanism linking livestream design features to consumer responses in fashion commerce and offer actionable guidance for streamer selection, interaction design, and the strategic framing of time bound promotions.​

detail.abstract:
Today, financial institutions are moving away from using automated decision support tools and are moving more and more towards using AI agents in their operations. Even as this improves the speed at which business is conducted, it is also changing the way decisions are made and, more importantly, whether these decisions can be explained, audited, and/or reconstructed. 

The implication for governance is significant. It is no longer possible to reverse engineer a decision made by the agent, audit the rationale behind the decision, and explain the rationale to those who need to know. This is creating significant trust deficits, particularly among the customer segment, who are most impacted by decisions made by the financial institution. 

The use of AI agents creates a significant competitive advantage, and this is what this paper terms as Intelligence Arbitrage, the ability of the financial institution to compress the time gap between signal and execution. The same compression, which is the basis for the creation of the concept of Intelligence Arbitrage, also creates a gap between the original purpose, intent, and strategy behind the financial institution and the decisions and outcomes created by the AI agents. This gap is what this paper terms as the Fiduciary Gap. 

The fiduciary Gap is not an abstract concept. The paper presents several financial events over the last few years, revealing a pattern of institutional outcomes, deviating from the intended strategic direction for which they were designed and optimized. To bridge this Fiduciary Gap, this paper introduces the concept of the Decision Velocity Engine, an institutional capability that can bridge the Fiduciary Gap without sacrificing the speed advantage that agents provide. It is based on an eight-layer control structure that we refer to as the Decision Integrity Chain™, which provides traceability from purpose to outcome and the ability to explain.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Understanding

detail.title: A Mathematical Theory of Understanding
detail.abstract:
Generative AI has transformed the economics of information production, making explanations, proofs, examples, and analyses available at very low cost. Yet the value of information still depends on whether downstream users can absorb and act on it. A signal conveys meaning only to a learner with the structural capacity to decode it: an explanation that clarifies a concept for one user may be indistinguishable from noise to another who lacks the relevant prerequisites. This paper develops a mathematical model of that learner side bottleneck.

We model the learner as a mind, an abstract learning system characterized by a prerequisite structure over concepts. A mind may represent a human learner, an artificial learner such as a neural network, or any agent whose ability to interpret signals depends on previously acquired concepts. Teaching is modeled as sequential communication with a latent target. Because instructional signals are usable only when the learner has acquired the prerequisites needed to parse them, the effective communication channel depends on the learner's current state of knowledge and becomes more informative as learning progresses. The model yields two limits on the speed of learning and adoption: a structural limit determined by prerequisite reachability and an epistemic limit determined by uncertainty about the target.

The framework implies threshold effects in training and capability acquisition. When the teaching horizon lies below the prerequisite depth of the target, additional instruction cannot produce successful completion of teaching; once that depth is reached, completion becomes feasible. This generates non-concave returns to training effort and implies that spreading scarce instructional resources evenly can yield lower output than concentrating them on fewer workers or users. Across heterogeneous learners, a common broadcast curriculum is slower than personalized instruction by a factor proportional to the number of learner types.

title: Axiograf: A Protocol for Machine-Verifiable Enterprise Action in the Age of Autonomous Firms

detail.title: Axiograf: A Protocol for Machine-Verifiable Enterprise Action in the Age of Autonomous Firms
detail.abstract:
This paper derives, from five primitive axioms concerning admissibility, a complete protocol architecture for machine-verifiable enterprise action. The derivation proceeds without empirical assumption, domain commitment, or temporal presupposition: from the logical structure of constraint alone.

The axiomatic foundation is Constraint-Induced Morphodynamics (CIMD). CIMD establishes that a system is constituted by its admissibility conditions; that constraints act solely by elimination, not by generation or preference; that non-invariant states cannot persist; and that stability is persistence under ordered re-evaluation, not under time. From these axioms a single derived statement follows necessarily: where admissibility conditions exist, non-invariant states cannot persist, admissible transitions therefore occur, and configurations that remain admissible across ordered evaluations constitute stable structure.

Axiograf is the operationalization of that derived statement as deployable enterprise infrastructure. Its architecture is not designed from observed practice — it is derived from the axioms. The three-layer structure of Canonical Fact Language, Adaptor Layer, and Constraint Layer follows necessarily from what the predicate C requires to be declared, evaluated, and verified. Constraints compile to stratified Datalog with bounded quantifiers — decidable, polynomial-time, and always explainable. A distributed stateless evaluator executes admissibility determinations at action time, producing cryptographically anchored Admissibility Records that serve as the complete evidentiary artifact of the protocol. A three-tier Constraint Registry with content-addressed versioning ensures every evaluation is permanently replayable. A cross-enterprise trust model enables independent verification without central authority and without prior agreement on policy content.

Together, CIMD and Axiograf constitute the missing admissibility substrate of the AI economy — the first infrastructure layer derived from first principles of admissibility rather than assembled from engineering convention.

detail.abstract: The accelerating global investment in artificial intelligence has created a structural problem that precedes any technical challenge: the information architecture surrounding AI decisions is fundamentally unbalanced. This paper introduces the concept of the AI Intelligence Deficit, defined as the systematic absence of independent, technically sophisticated expertise at the point where organisations commit capital and operational resources to AI initiatives. Drawing on market data indicating that 95% of enterprise AI pilots fail to deliver measurable returns and 42% of organisations abandoned the majority of their AI initiatives in 2025, the paper presents two original analytical frameworks. The Information Ecosystem Map classifies AI information sources across two dimensions, commercial incentive and technical expertise, revealing that the sources producing the highest volume of content possess the lowest independence, while sources with the deepest expertise generate the least content. The Signal Degradation Curve traces how AI capability claims deteriorate as they pass through successive layers of the information ecosystem, from original research findings through vendor interpretation, media translation, and cultural absorption. The paper examines high-profile failures including Builder.ai and nate as symptomatic of a market where the intelligence required for sound decisions is structurally absent from the channels that reach decision-makers. The analysis proposes three disciplines for closing the deficit: source awareness, signal tracing, and independent intelligence access.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely promoted as a means of enhancing efficiency, transparency, and service delivery in the public sector. In many developing countries, like Cameroon, Vietnam and Uganda, AI has not yet been embedded in core administrative functions. Instead, governments are primarily engaged in administrative reforms such as business process re-engineering (BPR), digitization, and organizational modernization. This study argues that the key challenge for algorithmic governance in Uganda lies not in AI adoption itself, but in institutional and organizational readiness. detail.abstract: This report analyzes the position of labor within debates about a just transition in the United States. detail.abstract: Brazil plays a critical role in the global environmental landscape due to its vast biodiversity, extensive forests, and substantial carbon stocks. Despite this relevance, its economy remains deeply dependent on commodity exports—particularly agricultural goods, crude oil, fuel oils, and iron ore—sectors historically linked to land concentration, socio-environmental conflicts, and significant impacts on Indigenous, Quilombola, and other Traditional communities. The election of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2022 renewed expectations that environmental protection would once again be placed at the centre of national policy, with commitments to expanding renewable energy, reversing deforestation, and promoting carbon capture and reforestation initiatives. title: Right over Might: Against Policy Space and toward Collective Enforcement in International Trade Law

detail.title: Right over Might: Against Policy Space and toward Collective Enforcement in International Trade Law
detail.abstract:
The paralysis of the WTO Appellate Body and the proliferation of self-judging national
security exceptions have precipitated calls to abandon strict rules-based discipline in favour
of expanded national policy space. Gregory Shaffer’s influential framework exemplifies this
approach, proposing that states be permitted to deploy proportionate unilateral measures to
rebalance structural distortions arising from the US–China economic rivalry. This paper
argues that legitimising such unilateral rebalancing is a dangerous concession that inflicts
substantive injustice on developing nations lacking the fiscal capacity to participate in
subsidy competition, legalises the trade vigilantism the WTO was designed to suppress,
erodes state accountability by sanctioning ex post departures from voluntarily assumed treaty
obligations, and rests on a proportionality analysis that is inherently subjective and practically
unworkable absent binding adjudication. The paper advances four interlocking institutional
proposals: an Interim Appellate Arbitration Mechanism to restore compulsory dispute
resolution; a Differentiated Subsidy Accountability Framework with tiered transparency
obligations and a reversed burden of proof; a Multilateral National Security Disciplines
Protocol codifying structured good faith review; and a Collective Countermeasure Protocol
that distributes retaliatory obligations through a GDP-proportional formula, transforming
enforcement from an individual vulnerability into a binding collective security commitment.
“Rightly constituted laws should be the final sovereign.”1 This Aristotelian ideal underpinned
the establishment of the World Trade Organization (WTO), promising a global order where
the right of legal adjudication would restrain the might of geopolitical power. For decades,
the Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) served as the guardian of this promise, binding
member states to a system where disputes were settled by international law rather than trade
wars. Yet today, that legal sovereign has been dethroned. The paralysis of the Appellate Body
and the aggressive expansion of self-judging National Security exceptions under the General
Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) Article XXI have unmoored the trading system from
its rules-based anchor. We are witnessing a reversion to G2 (US and China) bargaining2,
where large economies exploit institutional opacity and asymmetric policy space to maximize
national advantage at the expense of the global commons. In this paper, I will argue that
validating this erosion through normative frameworks of policy space as advocated by
Gregory Shaffer3 is a dangerous concession. Rather than saving the system, such an approach
induces substantive injustice to the developing nations, risks legalizing the very vigilantism
the WTO was designed to suppress, and erodes the regime of state accountability that helps
maintain international order. Shaffer’s proposed remedy is also arbitrary and would thus be
ineffectual in implementation.

detail.abstract: CONTEXTClimate change and market volatility are intensifying pressures on Australian agriculture, creating an urgent imperative for farmers and advisors to develop adaptive strategies.OBJECTIVEWe examined agricultural knowledge networks in the Central Tablelands region of New South Wales, where farmers recently endured severe drought, devastating bushfires, floods, and the COVID-19 pandemic.METHODSUsing social network analysis combined with semi-structured interviews, we investigated how farmers and farm advisors seek, evaluate, and share information to support adaptation.RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONSOur mixed-methods analysis of farmers and agricultural advisors revealed distinct networking strategies. Those we labelled “Rural CEOs” maintain low-homophily networks that link diverse types of agents, positioning these individuals as potential knowledge brokers. Constrained farmers operate within dense, homophilous networks that link like-minded farmers, thereby limiting their exposure to novel practices. Stewards demonstrate extensive networks with moderate homophily, whilst Farm Advisors exhibit unexpectedly high homophily, primarily connecting with colleagues rather than bridging diverse knowledge domains. The network structure reveals sparse connectivity, low centralisation, high clustering, and limited brokerage capacity. Values significantly shape networking strategies: Openness to Change drives homophilous innovation clusters, Self-transcendence motivates strategic heterophilous bridging, and Conservatism supports diverse information gathering. Farm ground cover index is correlated with tie formation, perhaps suggesting feedback between land management outcomes and networks. Digital information sources facilitate tie formation, whilst social media plays a surprisingly limited role despite its prominence in extension strategies.SIGNIFICANCEThese findings reveal misalignments between extension practices and farmers' demonstrated information-seeking behaviours, highlighting opportunities to reposition key actors as knowledge brokers whilst diversifying communication channels.

This paper examines the design implications of translation drift in institutional environments increasingly mediated by digital artefacts and AI systems. It argues that contemporary governance infrastructures—such as templates, criteria frameworks, scoring models, dashboards, and algorithmic systems—function not only as decision supports but as meaning infrastructures that stabilise and propagate institutional interpretations over time. As strategic intent is translated across governance layers, these artefacts shape how meaning is interpreted, operationalised, and reinforced, often introducing gradual shifts that remain invisible in outcome-based monitoring. The paper outlines design principles for governing interpretation in AI-mediated decision systems, emphasising the need to preserve fidelity to intent under conditions of scale, complexity, and delayed feedback. 
This paper forms part of the research programme The Coherence Problem: How Institutions Learn, Drift, and Realign, which studies institutional decision systems as interpretive learning systems.

detail.abstract: The consideration of CSR issues basically leads to reconsidering and/or extending many acknowledged positions and results in accounting research. detail.abstract: This study provides a systematic examination and critical evaluation of prevailing methodologies for incorporating risk into investment appraisal and project planning. It advances the argument that inadequate recognition or improper integration of risk-often arising from the use of flawed or overly complex analytical models-can materially distort decision outcomes and undermine project viability. Using a desk-research approach, the study analyzes cash-flow estimates from five projects drawn from the authors' tutorial archive. The project parameters were assessed using discounted cash-flow (DCF) techniques and risk metrics generated through Monte Carlo simulation, Mean-Relative Regression (MRR) analysis, and Enyi's simplified statistical risk model, which also produced the distribution of risk around mean cash flows. The findings reveal that the more sophisticated models not only pose practical challenges in application but also yield inconsistent results. In contrast, the risk-distribution insights produced by Enyi's simplified statistical model offer clearer, more coherent guidance for investment planning and project-appraisal decision makers. The study contributes to the literature by highlighting the value of simplified, transparent risk-integration frameworks in enhancing the reliability of capital-investment decisions.

title: Food on Road: How Road Density Lowers Food Price -Evidence from Urban Demand, Retail Structure, and Spatial Spillovers
affiliations: New Jersey Institute of Technology, NJIT and New Jersey Institute of Technology

detail.title: Food on Road: How Road Density Lowers Food Price -Evidence from Urban Demand, Retail Structure, and Spatial Spillovers
detail.abstract: Recent inflation in food prices have severely exacerbated the global food crisis and contributed to nationwide diet-related health challenges in the United States. This study investigates how transportation infrastructure, measured by road density, affects local food prices. Using U.S. county-level panel data from 2010 and 2020, supplemented with demographic and geographic controls, we reveal that greater road density significantly reduces meal costs by facilitating local and regional food mobility. Ceteris paribus, an additional mile of road per square mile is associated leads to a 1.3% decline in the cost per meal. This price-reducing effect is further shown to be heterogeneous. In particular, it becomes weaker in counties with high store density or large populations. Spatially, proximity to urban centers also attenuates the impact of road density on food prices. Moreover, our results indicate that road density generates spillover effects on surrounding countiesâ food prices. These findings shed light on how transportation infrastructure affects food mobility and pricing equity, offering evidence-based implications for urban planners, transportation policymakers, and local governments. The study makes several salient contributions to existing literature. First, it documents empirical evidence from the U.S. market on how infrastructure affects food prices, along with other geographic, demographic, and temporal factors. Second, the study offers a nuanced and in-depth understanding of how transportation networks interact with the local food market, spatially and temporally. Last but not least, this study enriches the food-transportation literature with a curated and shareable county-level road density dataset. Future research has been delineated, such as the impact of AgriTech (e.g., Vertical Farming) on food miles and prices.

title: A Unified Theory of Strategic and Tactical Asset Allocation
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: A Unified Theory of Strategic and Tactical Asset Allocation
detail.abstract: We develop a rigorous theoretical framework that unifies strategic asset allocation (SAA) and tactical asset allocation (TAA) within a single dynamic optimisation problem. In a continuous-time economy with regime-switching asset dynamics and Epstein-Zin recursive utility, we prove that the optimal portfolio admits a unique decomposition into a myopic component-which we identify as the regimeconditional SAA-and a hedging demand component-which we identify as the TAA. The TAA emerges endogenously from the investor's desire to hedge against future regime transitions, rather than from ad-hoc market-timing overlays. We establish performance bounds linking both regime-detection accuracy and moment estimation error to expected utility loss, and derive a formal partial-adjustment rule for TAA under quadratic trading costs, providing a principled answer to the question of when TAA adds value. A multi-scale signal decomposition via nested filtrations provides an orthogonal variance attribution across SAA, TAA, and alpha overlay components. Our results nest several existing models as special cases and generate testable empirical predictions.

title: Partial Information in Fork-join Operations: Evidence from Multi-brand Cloud Kitchens
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore and Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Ahmedabad

detail.title: Partial Information in Fork-join Operations: Evidence from Multi-brand Cloud Kitchens
detail.abstract: Multi-brand cloud kitchens offer variety by co-locating multiple restaurant brands, allowing customers to order across brands in a single order. To simplify ordering, platforms also offer pre-designed dish combinations, created by listing one brand's dish on another brand's menu. Using 6.24 million orders from a multi-brand operator in Asia (68 kitchens), we document a significant operational penalty: multi-brand orders are 48% more likely to be late than single-brand orders and receive lower ratings in our sample. Field visits and interviews indicate that fulfillment in these kitchens is a fork-join process wherein dishes are produced in parallel at brand stations and synchronized by a kitchen officer, and the pre-designed combinations create information asymmetry requiring chefs' coordination. Reduced-form estimates show orders with pre-designed combinations are 32% more likely to be late than orders requiring only synchronization. Brand ownership also matters. Combining dishes from two in-house brands benefits from faster synchronization relative to combining external and in-house brands, but higher congestion at in-house stations erodes this advantage. Finally, counterfactual analysis shows that information sharing and prioritization may be complements: providing complete information improves performance when the platform prioritizes multi-brand orders, whereas under partial information, FIFO can yield lower delays and better quality outcomes.

title: Climate Litigation as Conversation: Courts, Climate and Legitimacy
affiliations: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid

detail.title: Climate Litigation as Conversation: Courts, Climate and Legitimacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare no conflicting interest in the elaboration of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study includes no participants. It is based on court cases that are in the public domain.
declarations.funderStatement: I am co-Principal Investigator in the Grant "Markets and Normative Consistency: Competition and Sustainability" (Grant no. PID2024-161496OB-I00) by the Spanish Ministry of Science.

detail.abstract: Climate litigation is widespread, important… and controversial. Climate lawsuits have attracted interest due to their social, economic, financial and governance implications. However, the question they raise is essentially, and existentially legal: should courts adjudicate climate policy? This article tries to answer that question. It argues that courts are not well placed to adjudicate under a traditional model of litigation where plaintiffs ask courts to allocate them concrete rights and prescribe specific outcomes. In fact, when disputes are framed in this way, courts tend to abstain from adjudicating or defer to other authorities. When they decide, they put their legitimacy at risk. However, a different model of litigation is possible, which this article labels "litigation as conversation". Under that model courts facilitate the discussion of climate facts and policy by public and private actors. They do so by, first, ensuring coherence between law, policy and execution, i.e., between what is promised, what is done, and what is lawful. Second, they can elicit information production, and verify the information produced, possibly the most important, and most overlooked function. Third, courts enable coordination and participation, fostering reflection through an iterative process. This model captures how courts try to engage in climate disputes (descriptive perspective), but it also provides arguments to critically assess whether, and when courts fall short of their duty, or go too far (normative perspective). Thus, "litigation as conversation" can help understand what courts do (and can do), and to buttress their role in climate disputes, and their legitimacy.

title: Accreditation as a Selection Technology in Health Care Markets

detail.title: Accreditation as a Selection Technology in Health Care Markets
detail.abstract: Accreditation is widely used in regulated health care markets and is typically viewed as an information device that mitigates asymmetric information and improves patient choice. In many institutional settings, however, accreditation also determines eligibility for insured reimbursement and network participation, thereby conditioning access to the principal source of demand. This paper studies the implications of that eligibility function. In a model with heterogeneous provider quality and heterogeneous patient risk, where higher-risk patients derive greater marginal benefit from higherquality care and adverse outcomes are often irreversible, conditioning access to insured patients on accreditation status changes the rule governing provider survival. When accreditation is not strictly rank-preserving in outcome-relevant treatment quality, survival need not be monotone in clinical effectiveness over the range in which eligibility is binding: higher-quality but non-accredited providers may exit, while accredited providers with lower treatment quality remain active. The analysis shows that this substitution of eligibility-based selection for outcome-based selection weakens risk-quality sorting and can reduce aggregate health production even under fully rational beliefs and informational improvement. Competitive pressure expands the region in which accreditation determines survival, and regulatory stringency may generate non-monotonic welfare effects when accreditation imperfectly tracks treatment effectiveness. The results highlight that accreditation policy in health care affects not only information and average quality, but the process of market selection and patient allocation that underlies health outcomes.

title: Ethical Considerations and Algorithmic Bias of Artificial Intelligence in Education
affiliations: Hurix Digital, Andheri, India

detail.title: Ethical Considerations and Algorithmic Bias of Artificial Intelligence in Education
detail.abstract: The fast adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the educational field has raised powerful questions about the bias, fairness, and ethical responsibility of algorithms, however, no thorough synthesis of overlapping questions has been developed. It is the systematic review of the ethical aspects and manifestations of bias of AI-based educational technologies published in the year 2019 to 2025. Based on the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, being aware of the 1,847 records sifted through Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and PubMed, 94 peer-reviewed articles were identified. The results show that algorithmic bias on AI-based learning systems is most likely to work against underrepresented racial, socioeconomic, and language students, and automated grading and predictive analytics systems can be characterized by quantifiable differences in the accuracy rate across demographic groups. They can be ethical issues such as the absence of transparency in the work of algorithmic decision-making, the absence of mechanisms of student data governance, and the lack of culturally responsive principles in designing AI. The review is also able to detect the promising mechanisms of creating equitable educational AI in the emerging opportunities in federated learning, explainable AI (XAI), and participatory design. Regulatory environments are still disjointed, and policy tools are not in line with implementation facts. The paper will summarize evidence in areas of application such as intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, admissions algorithms, and adaptive content delivery to shape the present ethical AI in education and propose a research agenda to realize equitable, transparent and responsible AI usage in the learning experience.

title: Use it or Slowly Lose it: Expertise Atrophy with Organizational AI Usage
affiliations: , Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business

detail.title: Use it or Slowly Lose it: Expertise Atrophy with Organizational AI Usage
detail.abstract: Problem definition: As organizations adopt generative AI, its use can improve productivity, but reliance can lead to atrophy of worker knowledge and skills. The challenge is how to incentivize human oversight and sustain long-run expertise. This is difficult because improving AI quality makes oversight and skill maintenance harder to motivate, as acceptable outcomes increasingly occur even when workers disengage. Methodology/results: Using a principal-agent framework, we study optimal incentive design when workers exert costly effort to verify imperfect AI output, where effort both improves current performance and preserves expertise. Three implications arise. First, profit-maximizing compensation can be non-monotonic in AI quality or skill, and firms may even be more profitable with worse AI systems. Second, due to contracting frictions, firms may allow expertise to deteriorate by substituting effort for expertise, leading to significant performance losses relative to a benchmark where both are prescribed. Third, when tasks are relatively less complex with short learning curves and high returns on effort for low-skilled workers, then the risk of skill atrophy can mitigate these frictions. For such tasks workers are self-motivated to preserve expertise, so higher rates of potential skill loss can, counterintuitively, increase profit. Managerial implications: We identify when strong incentives are needed to sustain engagement and maintain expertise, and when contracting frictions create tension in providing them. In doing so, we call out potential AI "danger zones." We discover that moderate-to-high AI performance requires stronger incentives for vigilance. When skill decay is low to moderate, expertise losses may be overlooked yet generate substantial long-term costs, underscoring when proactive monitoring and investment in human capital are most valuable.

title: Breaking the Silence: A Socio-Psychological Analysis of Mental Health Stigma in Bangladesh

detail.title: Breaking the Silence: A Socio-Psychological Analysis of Mental Health Stigma in Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
Mental health stigma remains a deeply rooted social challenge in Bangladesh, shaped by cultural norms, religious interpretations, and concerns about social identity. This study seeks to understand how stigma surrounding mental illness is experienced, expressed, and sustained within everyday social contexts. Based on 25 in-depth interviews and two focus group discussions conducted in urban and semi-urban areas of Dhaka, Chattogram, and Rajshahi, the research adopts a qualitative approach to capture lived experiences and community narratives.

The analysis draws on Social Identity Theory, Attribution Theory, Labeling Theory, and Allport’s Contact Hypothesis to provide a socio psychological perspective on how individuals interpret mental illness and how stigma becomes embedded in social relationships. Using Braun and Clarke’s six step thematic analysis framework, the findings indicate that stigma is largely driven by fear of social labeling, widespread misconceptions about mental health conditions, and concerns about family honor and social reputation. These factors often discourage open discussion and delay help seeking behavior.

At the same time, the study identifies signs of change. Supportive family members, engaged faith leaders, and growing advocacy initiatives show that stigma is not fixed or unchangeable. Through sustained dialogue, awareness building, and inclusive community engagement, alternative understandings of mental health are gradually emerging. The study concludes by recommending culturally responsive strategies such as peer led support networks, tele psychiatry services, and art based advocacy initiatives to reduce stigma and strengthen community based mental health resilience in Bangladesh.

title: Are We Ready? From Vocabulary Switch to Regime Switch in Disclosure Demand
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Are We Ready? From Vocabulary Switch to Regime Switch in Disclosure Demand
detail.abstract: Public debate surrounding unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) frequently centers on a practical policy demand: disclosure. While some observers actively advocate for immediate disclosure, a substantial share of the population currently devotes little attention to the issue. This paper examines how shifts in public attention may influence the evolution of disclosure demand. The analysis considers a population composed of attentive agents who support disclosure and cannot-care-right-now (CCRN) agents who remain largely inattentive. Government communications-including hearings, reports, and related signals-may shift individuals from the CCRN group into the attentive population. The model predicts that when attention activation interacts with social influence, the system may transition rapidly toward a common consensus supporting disclosure once a sufficient share of previously inattentive individuals becomes attentive. The paper therefore examines whether institutions are prepared for the possibility that increased public attention could trigger very rapid convergence of public opinion toward a disclosure demand.

detail.abstract: Modern institutions face a subtle but pervasive challenge: as decisions are translated across layers of governance, meaning can gradually shift, allowing organizations to perform successfully while drifting from their original intent. This paper advances a general theory of institutional coherence centred on the concept of the Sovereign Spine—the structured sequence through which purpose is translated into priorities, criteria, actions, and signals over time. It argues that coherence is not maintained primarily through central control, but emerges from distributed interpretive processes as meaning moves through decision systems. Building on prior work on translation drift, observability, and governance design, the paper synthesises these mechanisms into a unified theoretical framework of distributed coherence. It introduces key constructs explaining how institutions preserve or lose fidelity to intent under conditions of complexity, delayed feedback, and AI-mediated decision-making. The contribution is to reconceptualise institutional alignment as a dynamic, system-level property of meaning translation rather than a static condition of agreement, providing a foundation for analysing institutional agency and designing governance systems capable of maintaining coherence over time.

detail.abstract: Sortation systems have emerged as a foundational technology in modern warehouse automation, enabling high-speed, high-accuracy routing of goods in e-commerce fulfillment, parcel logistics, and distribution centers. This paper examines the operational architecture, technological components, and strategic importance of automated sortation systems. It explores how barcode and RFID identification, conveyor-based material handling, and intelligent warehouse control software integrate to optimize throughput and reduce human dependency. The study further analyzes system types including cross-belt, tilt-tray, pouch, and line sorters and evaluates their benefits in productivity, accuracy, and workplace safety. Through industry case examples, the paper demonstrates measurable improvements in efficiency and scalability. The research concludes that sortation systems are not merely mechanical tools but strategic infrastructure investments essential to the evolution of digital logistics ecosystems.

title: Impact of Affordable AI-Based Hybrid Learning Devices on Primary Education and Regional Economic Growth
affiliations: VSSD College Kanpur and VSSD College Kanpur

detail.title: Impact of Affordable AI-Based Hybrid Learning Devices on Primary Education and Regional Economic Growth
detail.abstract:
The research adopts an integrative literature review and conceptual analysis approach. International studies on AI-supported education are synthesized alongside principles of educational psychology, particularly Bloom’s 3H framework (Head, Heart, Hand), to construct a context-sensitive model suitable for Indian primary education. Rather than relying on statistical datasets, the study employs logical reasoning, psychological theory, global educational trends, and expert judgment to assess the feasibility, educational relevance, and potential impact of the proposed device.

Conceptual findings indicate that such hybrid learning systems can strengthen cognitive development, analytical thinking, learner engagement, and problem-solving abilities at the foundational stage. Beyond educational outcomes, the model highlights two significant socio-economic implications: the possibility of employment generation through local manufacturing and device assembly, and the enhancement of regional digital literacy contributing to a future-ready workforce.

The study concludes that low-cost AI-enabled hybrid learning devices have the potential to reduce digital inequality while simultaneously supporting regional economic development. The proposed framework offers practical insights for educators and policymakers seeking scalable, inclusive, and cost-effective technology-driven solutions for strengthening primary education.

title: Progress in Employee Participation? A Critical Analysis of Board-level Employee Representation in China's New Company Law
