detail.title: Does Employment Shift Mothers' Voting Behavior and Political Identity?
detail.abstract:
While the correlation between working and voting is positive, I provide the first causal evidence that this relationship is negative. Using five decades of Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) expansions and 1990s welfare reform as instruments for employment, I find that working lowers voter turnout and increases conservatism among lower-income mothers. Voter registration, political knowledge, and civic engagement decline, while preferences for conservative policies rise. Effects are largest for unmarried, younger, and less-educated mothers and are substantially stronger outside metropolitan areas. Notably, political shifts are concentrated among White women despite larger employment gains among non-White women, driven in part by White women entering more conservative coworker environments. Prior exposure to work also matters: women without working mothers experience larger ideological shifts. While recent decades have seen more women voting Democrat, even more women would have voted Democrat if not for decades of pro-work public policy targeting lower-income mothers.

title: Improve Enterprise Financial Fraud by Time-Consistent Equilibrium Insurance-Reinsurance Strategy

detail.title: Improve Enterprise Financial Fraud by Time-Consistent Equilibrium Insurance-Reinsurance Strategy
detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often face severe financing constraints due to high credit risk and information asymmetry. To mitigate credit risk and facilitate SME financing, insurance and reinsurance mechanisms can be introduced into the credit market to enhance risk sharing and monitoring incentives. Our research develops a hierarchical Stackelberg game model to study the interaction among enterprises, banks, insurance companies, reinsurance companies, and government regulators. The framework integrates the vertical credit relationship between banks and enterprises with insurer-reinsurer risk-sharing arrangements, allowing fraud incentives, default risk, and regulatory enforcement to be analyzed within a unified equilibrium structure. The model is formulated in a discrete-time finite-horizon setting under a time-consistent equilibrium control framework. We characterize the equilibrium strategies of the financial sector and the optimal regulatory policy through backward induction. The results show that insurance-reinsurance arrangements enhance monitoring incentives, reduce equilibrium fraud incidence, and lower the regulatory intensity required to deter fraudulent behavior. Moreover, endogenous reinsurance participation improves welfare and reduces default risk relative to the benchmark without insurance. These findings highlight the role of reinsurance mechanisms in improving financial discipline and risk sharing in credit-financing systems.

title: When Are Decisions Improvable? An Evaluation of Diagnostic Methods
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, , California Institute of Technology (Caltech) and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management

detail.title: When Are Decisions Improvable? An Evaluation of Diagnostic Methods
detail.abstract:
We evaluate three methods for identifying improvable choices: documenting specific misconceptions (the Characterization Assessment method), gauging confidence in choices (the Decision Confidence method), and showing that specific behavioral patterns in the domain of interest also emerge in a related domain where they are objectively suboptimal (the Pattern Matching method). In experiments involving risky choice, the three methods imply that different choices are improvable and have conflicting implications regarding legitimate risk preferences. We clarify the assumptions underlying each method and reevaluate the evidence on risk-taking in light of their limitations.

title: An 'Austrian' Model of International Specialization
affiliations: Harvard University - Department of Economics and Harvard University

detail.title: An 'Austrian' Model of International Specialization
detail.abstract:
We develop a general equilibrium model of international trade in which the temporal structure of production is a key determinant of comparative advantage. Building on Böhm-Bawerk’s theory of capital, the model formalizes the idea that production processes with longer average periods of production (APPs) entail higher financing costs due to the time lag between input payments and revenue realization. We embed this insight into a multi-sector Ricardian framework with endogenous interest rates. Under autarky, countries with more patient consumers or more developed financial markets exhibit lower equilibrium interest rates and higher wage rates. With international trade, these countries typically gain a comparative advantage in sectors with longer APPs, though the model can also generate multiple equilibria and unconventional specialization patterns. We extend the framework to include trade costs (inclusive of shipment delays), global value chains, and international capital-market integration. Empirically, we present evidence showing that countries with more developed financial systems export disproportionately more in sectors with longer APPs, even after controlling for standard neoclassical and institutional determinants of comparative advantage.

title: The Localism Act 2011: The Hollow Housing Law Revolution

detail.title: The Localism Act 2011: The Hollow Housing Law Revolution
detail.abstract: In November 2011, the Localism Act was passed and, on one view, reflects the widest-ranging reforms to housing law for over a half century. Ambitious in its stated aims, the legislation was trailed as representing a broad shift in power from central Whitehall to local communities and individuals. The article critically examines the central changes introduced by the 2011 Act as they pertain specifically to housing law in England, namely the new flexible tenancy regime, the changes to homelessness duties under Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 and the reforms concerning the allocation of social housing. The article interrogates the extent to which the reforms realise the stated localist agenda and highlights areas of difficulty in interpretation and application. It concludes that rather than bestowing greater power on local communities, the reforms to housing law will instead effect a perceptible reduction of power in the hands of local people.

title: Rolling Windows, Closed Doors: Mobility and Tenure Effects of Oregon's Statewide Rent Stabilization Policy

detail.title: Rolling Windows, Closed Doors: Mobility and Tenure Effects of Oregon's Statewide Rent Stabilization Policy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal effects of Oregon Senate Bill 608 (SB608), the first statewide rent stabilization law in United States history, on residential mobility and homeownership. Exploiting the law's age-based exemption, which excludes buildings younger than 15 years from coverage, I use a rolling window difference in differences design applied to 580,897 ACS household observations. I find that rent stabilization reduces residential mobility in covered buildings by 10-36 percent relative to pre-policy baselines. Covered buildings also exhibit relative increases in homeownership of 5-6 percent. These effects emerge despite SB608's comparatively permissive rent cap (7 percent plus CPI), suggesting that landlords and tenants respond to the existence of a stabilization regime even when caps do not immediately bind. Of 56 estimated specifications, 29 (52%) pass both pre-trends and placebo validity tests, demonstrating the robustness of results to specification choice. These results extend prior findings of city-level evidence to a statewide setting and reveal unintended consequences for housing supply and tenure composition.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
detail.abstract:
We use novel data from a survey of nearly 750 corporate executives to study the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on productivity and the workforce. We document substantial heterogeneity in AI adoption across firms, with more than half having already invested, though many smaller firms are only beginning to do so. Labor productivity gains are positive, vary across sectors, and are expected to strengthen in 2026, with the largest effects concentrated in high-skill services and finance. These gains are not primarily driven by firms' capital deepening but instead reflect increases in revenue-based total factor productivity, closely associated with innovation-and demand-oriented channels. We document a productivity paradox, in which perceived productivity gains are larger than measured productivity gains, likely reflecting a delay in revenue realizations. In labor markets, we find little evidence of near-term aggregate employment declines due to AI, though larger companies anticipate AI-driven workforce reductions, while smaller firms expect modest gains. We also find evidence of compositional reallocation of labor both within and across firms, with routine clerical roles declining and a relative demand for skilled technical roles increasing. We develop an index that ranks job functions most negatively affected by AI.

title: Circular Flow Model for Agentic AI: Recursive Risk, Autonomy, and Operational Instability

detail.title: Circular Flow Model for Agentic AI: Recursive Risk, Autonomy, and Operational Instability
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence shifts from static inference toward autonomous agency, traditional linear governance and risk frameworks are becoming increasingly inadequate. Agentic AI systems reason, plan, act, and learn within recursive decision loops, repeatedly ingesting the consequences of their own actions. This paper introduces the Circular Flow Model as a conceptual framework for understanding how risk emerges, compounds, and propagates across these autonomous cycles. By analysing the stages of Input, Model, Output, and Action as an interconnected control loop, the paper shows how small errors can accumulate into feedback-driven instability, leading to behavioural drift and operational loss of control. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes a four-domain governance framework-Structural, Execution, Memory, and Assurance guardrails-designed to bound autonomy, preserve system integrity, and maintain accountability in real-world deployments. The model provides a practical lens for organisations seeking to manage recursive risk and operational instability as AI systems transition from tools to autonomous actors.

title: Alternative Basel Capital Formula: Insights from 20 Years of Bank Loss Data
affiliations: VU Amsterdam

detail.title: Alternative Basel Capital Formula: Insights from 20 Years of Bank Loss Data
detail.abstract:
The Basel II capital formula and the surrounding academic discourse it have primarily focused on asset correlation derived from defaults. This study applies an alternative asymptotic single risk factor (ASRF) model in which the parameterization of the asset correlation is derived from loss time series rather than from observed default frequencies (“ODF”) or loss given default (“LGD”) time series using method-of-moments with a block bootstrap approach. With 20 years of loss data collected by large international banks, integration of ODF and LGD data to analyze historical losses directly, has become possible. This
approach offers several advantages. First, capital is intended to absorb losses — not defaults. Second, the approach enables the consistent measurement of conditional PD and conditional LGD using the same framework. Third, it allows for the inclusion of correlations between PD and LGD. Finally, the downturn LGD requirement in the capital formula is eliminated, thereby reducing complexity for both supervisors and banks. Rather than focusing solely on the level of asset correlation, this study also investigates the relationship between asset correlation and loan types—such as junior and senior loans with various types of collateral. The findings result in an ASRF model that allows capital to be calculated at the loan level using the following inputs: through-the-cycle (TTC) PD, TTC LGD, loan type, collateral type, and small- and medium enterprise (“SME”) indicator. Our findings indicate that senior unsecured loans exhibit a downturn LGD of 59%, thus significantly exceeding Basel’s 40%-45% assumption under the Foundation Approach. At the same time, the new ASRF modelyields substantially lower risk weights than those imposed by Basel, thereby confirming the inconsistency in how PD and LGD are treated in the current Basel framework.

title: Contract Enforcement and Young Firm Capital Structure: A Global Perspective
affiliations: University of New Hampshire and University of California - Davis

detail.title: Contract Enforcement and Young Firm Capital Structure: A Global Perspective
detail.abstract:
We develop a framework to measure the severity of financial constraints for young firms across countries. Using ORBIS balance-sheet data for 23 economies, we show that short-term leverage rises while long-term leverage falls early in firms’ life cycles, with this pattern persisting longer where contract enforcement is weaker. We build a model of optimal financing under limited enforcement with endogenous debt maturity and blueprint capacity that matches these patterns and enables structural measurement of financial constraints. The framework decomposes the funding gap into within-firm borrowing constraints that ease with repayment history and a scale distortion identifiable through cross-country comparisons.

detail.abstract:
While the 2025 Nobel Prize recognized the power of creative destruction in driving economic growth, we present a market process theory demonstrating that destruction is not necessary. Through systematic resource coupling, creative construction achieves Pareto-optimal growth, expansion where all stakeholders benefit simultaneously without incumbent displacement, government subsidies, or social safety net costs.

The Tawfiki Market Process Theory, grounded in Israel M. Kirzner's Austrian market process economics, introduces the (*) operator, a mathematical representation of entrepreneurial discovery efficiency in coupling underutilized assets across economic sectors. The core equation, Rd = (D)* × (Po), transforms traditional ratio-based financial metrics into product-based relationships, generating five variations that maintain equivalence with corporate finance formulas while producing leverage-neutral returns where ROE = ROA.

We present empirical validation from live market implementations in Jamaica (2010-2025): a restaurant-telecommunications coupling demonstrating 12.5× value leverage, and a comprehensive taxi-housing-energy integration achieving 50.7× coupling multipliers. Both cases satisfy a rigorous Zero-Sum Test Protocol confirming genuine Pareto outcomes with no hidden subsidies or regulatory arbitrage.

The framework's mathematical innovation lies in Po cancellation, which eliminates capital structure dependency, fundamentally diverging from the Du Pont Identity at precisely the point where leverage-based returns separate from discovery-based returns. This represents the first rigorous mathematical formalization of Austrian economics, operationalizing Kirzner's concepts of entrepreneurial alertness, spontaneous order, and dispersed knowledge aggregation into quantifiable, testable predictions.

Conservative estimates suggest $2.9 trillion in potential global efficiency gains over 15 years across five major sector couplings (housing-energy, food service-telecommunications, agriculture-logistics-finance, education-employment-housing, and healthcare-transportation-nutrition). The theory provides policy implications favouring market-driven coordination over centralized planning, with zero fiscal burden compared to creative destruction's $50-100 billion annual social cost (U.S. scale).

We acknowledge significant limitations: small empirical sample size (n=2), single-country geographic concentration, lack of peer-reviewed validation, and requirement for entrepreneurial discovery capabilities that may not universalize. The framework applies specifically where underutilization indices satisfy UI₁ × UI₂ > 1% threshold and complementarity scores exceed 0.7, establishing clear boundary conditions.

title: Institutional Trust, Horizontal Equity, and Tax Morale in India

detail.title: Institutional Trust, Horizontal Equity, and Tax Morale in India
detail.abstract: I examine how institutional trust and perceptions of fairness across taxpayer groups may influence tax morale in India using data from the World Values Survey. Tax morale, defined as the intrinsic motivation to pay taxes, is an important factor shaping tax compliance. I find a positive and statistically significant association between tax morale and trust in the government, parliament, and civil services. Salaried employees report lower tax morale than self-employed individuals. This pattern contrasts with much of the existing empirical literature and is interpreted through the lens of horizontal equity. In settings with a narrow personal income tax base and variation in income reporting and monitoring across taxpayer groups, perceived differences in effective tax burdens may weaken tax morale of salaried employees. The findings highlight the role of institutional quality and horizontal equity in sustaining voluntary tax compliance.

title: Analytical Demand Management: How To Minimize Tied-Up Capital And Maximize Conversion In Retail And Service Businesses Through Customer Intake Micro-Processes

detail.title: Analytical Demand Management: How To Minimize Tied-Up Capital And Maximize Conversion In Retail And Service Businesses Through Customer Intake Micro-Processes
detail.abstract: Traditional management literature often associates business growth with increased sales volume, market expansion, or productive capacity enhancement. However, such an approach frequently overlooks a central factor for the economic sustainability of small businesses: efficiency in capital allocation. This article proposes a model of analytical demand management based on the systematization of initial customer intake micro-processes and the analysis of suppressed demand, defined as situations in which customer purchase intention does not convert into sales due to misalignment between offer, inventory, or operational capacity. The study is grounded in a proprietary database comprising more than 21,000 real customer intake records, collected longitudinally between 2023 and 2026, reflecting actual interactions between small businesses and their customers. The findings demonstrate that reducing tied-up capital and increasing conversion rates do not depend solely on higher sales volume, but rather on the ability to identify, measure, and correct recurring patterns of revenue loss. This research contributes to the entrepreneurship and applied management literature by presenting a replicable framework for data-driven decision-making based on real operational data, with direct impact on liquidity, financial predictability, and organizational sustainability.

detail.abstract: Dynamic capabilities theory calls for cognitive micro-foundations but leaves unspecified the reasoning practice through which architectural reconfiguration occurs. This article introduces firstprinciples thinking as that missing micro-foundation and derives the complementarity thesis: under identifiable scope conditions, organisations operating from first-principles-derived constraint spaces can generate exploitation and exploration as joint outputs of the same cognitive investment, substantially relaxing the trade-off ambidexterity theory treats as structural. A five-stage pipeline operationalises the practice and epistemic infrastructure specifies its institutional preconditions. A provisional diagnostic instrument, the Foundational Robustness Diagnostic, is offered as a scaffold for future empirical validation.

title: When ChatGPT Stops Talking: GenAI-induced Retail Herding and Systematic Risk

detail.title: When ChatGPT Stops Talking: GenAI-induced Retail Herding and Systematic Risk
detail.abstract: Using 21 unexpected ChatGPT outages as exogenous shocks to GenAI availability, we study how GenAI adoption affects retail investors' collective behavioral biases and market quality. We find that ChatGPT acts as a "belief homogenizer," synchronizing retail beliefs and trading decisions. This synchronization reflects collective overreaction rather than a collective-level improvement in information processing. ChatGPT availability worsens market liquidity by crowding out retail investors' natural contrarian liquidity-provision role. We further show that ChatGPT threatens market stability by aggregating idiosyncratic retail noise into undiversifiable systematic risk.

title: Beyond Capabilities: Durability Economics And The Providence Value Unit

detail.title: Beyond Capabilities: Durability Economics And The Providence Value Unit
detail.abstract: Economic theory has progressively expanded its evaluative scope from welfare outcomes to capabilities and institutional performance. Yet a fundamental dimension of economic life remains comparatively underexplored: whether economic institutions preserve the durability of meaningful human agency across time. Existing frameworks evaluate what economic systems produce, what opportunities they make available, and how governance structures shape incentives. None systematically examines whether institutions sustain the temporal conditions under which longterm human action remains intelligible across generations. This article introduces Durability Economics as a conceptual framework concerned with the institutional conditions that preserve or undermine the continuity of meaningful human agency across time. Within this framework, it proposes the Providence Value Unit (PVU) as a conceptual metric for evaluating agency durability-not as a measure of output or welfare, but as a composite assessment of whether the biological, demographic, institutional, monetary, and material systems of a society sustain the temporal credibility of human action across generations. The article traces the evolution of economic evaluation from welfare economics through Sen's capability approach and North's institutional economics; identifies agency durability as the missing analytical dimension in all three traditions; introduces the concepts of temporal plausibility of agency, agency fragility, and temporal credibility as the theoretical core of Durability Economics; develops the PVU formula PVU = f(B,H,C,D,F,G,M,S,I,T) across ten structural pillars; situates Durability Economics in relation to civilizational production functions; and integrates the framework with the author's complementary analytical contributions-TRIDO-AA, Decision-Time Accessibility (DTA), and Decision-Time Retrieval Failure (DTRF)-into a multi-level architecture of agency analysis.

title: Reviving the Military's Term Limit
affiliations: Emory University School of Law and

detail.title: Reviving the Military's Term Limit

publicationDetails.journalName: Emory University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This Article argues for the revival of a dormant constitutional safeguard that the Framers intended to keep the military accountable to the people.  The safeguard is the Constitution’s forgotten Two-Year Clause, which prohibits Congress from appropriating funds “to raise and support Armies” for a period longer than two years.  Intended to be Congress’s peace power, a 1904 legal opinion by Solicitor General William Hoyt strictly limiting the reach of the clause led to its obsolescence during the twentieth century.  Congresses now routinely appropriate long-term funding for the Army, thereby putting important functions beyond the influence of their successors.  The 119th Congress, for example, put military immigration enforcement and detention beyond the reach of the soon-to-be elected 120th Congress by providing four-year money for those activities in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.  

The Article makes the affirmative case for reviving the Two-Year Clause on originalism, separation of powers, and federalism grounds.  Hoyt’s opinion and the practice of routine long-term and permanent army appropriations it has enabled are contrary to the original meaning and intent of the constitution as well as early congressional practice.  Moreover, reviving the Two-Year Clause would strengthen the separation of powers by preserving a fast-eroding norm of annual and biennial appropriations for most military functions while enhancing congressional control over the important subset of functions subject to long-term appropriations.  Doing so would also protect state sovereignty as to domestic deployments of federal armies—whether called the “Army” or not—by re-engaging the political safeguards of federalism. 

National security, historical gloss, and justiciability considerations that have neutralized other checks on the president’s war powers should not stand in the way of reviving the Two-Year Clause.  Revival would not have operational effects on national security decision-making and its fiscal effects would be mixed.  Revival would not conflict with courts’ use of historical gloss in interpreting other war powers because the Two-Year Clause is distinctive in specifically prohibiting any one Congress from surrendering the power it guarantees to every Congress.  And revival would not force courts to second-guess sensitive military judgments because the clause renders legislation unconstitutional, not executive action.

title: The Motherhood Penalty in the Mutual Fund Industry
affiliations: University of Mannheim - Finance Area, Australian National University (ANU), University of Mannheim - Finance Area and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Motherhood Penalty in the Mutual Fund Industry
detail.abstract: Using mandatory maternity-leave disclosures for Chinese mutual fund managers, we estimate the career effects of childbirth in a setting with observable performance. Comparing new mothers to their pre-birth co-managers on the same funds, we find large and persistent penalties: mothers are 42% less likely to remain in the industry and, conditional on staying, hold 26% fewer leadership roles and manage 38% less (normalized) assets. Performance falls temporarily during pregnancy but quickly rebounds after birth, and investor flows do not decline. Career penalties outlast and exceed temporary performance effects, pointing to frictions in post-leave retention and responsibility allocation.

title: Nostalgic Messaging-Driven Turnout Analysis: Transformer-Based Detection and Temporal Causal Modeling of Political Ad Effects in Battleground States

detail.title: Nostalgic Messaging-Driven Turnout Analysis: Transformer-Based Detection and Temporal Causal Modeling of Political Ad Effects in Battleground States
detail.abstract: Contrary to laboratory predictions of nostalgic mobilization, this field study finds no overall relationship between nostalgic advertising and voter turnout across 393 battleground counties, establishing boundary conditions for nostalgic appeals. We classified 450 presidential campaign advertisements from 2020 and 2024 across five battleground states (Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Michigan, Georgia, Arizona) using a fine-tuned DistilBERT transformer model pre-trained on an augmented corpus of 400 political speech excerpts from the Miller Center Presidential Speech Archive and validated with 5-fold cross-validation (F1 = 0.91, AUC = 0.92), achieving superior discrimination over dictionary-based and logistic regression baselines. Using a pre-post change design following difference-indifferences logic, we tested whether nostalgic advertising increases predicted turnout gains. The overall association was not significant (ρ = 0.065, p = 0.197; 95% CI [-0.038, 0.171]) and remained null across bootstrap resampling, permutation tests, and regression with demographic controls. However, Georgia showed a significant negative effect (ρ =-0.298, p < 0.001), driven entirely by White-majority counties (ρ =-0.406, p < 0.001) while below-median White counties showed no relationship (ρ = 0.028, p = 0.806). Event study analysis across seven elections (2000-2024) confirmed parallel pre-treatment trends, with negative divergence emerging only after eight years of MAGA messaging. These demographic patterns, interpreted alongside Georgia's rapid suburban realignment and advertising wear-out theory, suggest diminishing returns to nostalgic political appeals in contexts of prolonged exposure, challenging laboratory predictions and identifying boundary conditions where nostalgic framing may backfire rather than mobilize.

detail.abstract: Background: Maternal mortality remains disproportionately high in low-resource settings, where the lack of specialized maternal care hinders early risk detection. While machine learning (ML) models offer a solution for automated risk stratification, they often struggle with class imbalance and limited interpretability. This study developed and evaluated an interpretable ML framework for three-level maternal risk classification to support clinical decision-making. Methods: We analyzed 786 de-identified maternal health records from rural Bangladesh, utilizing six routine variables: age, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, and heart rate. The pipeline applied Yeo-Johnson transformations and cost-sensitive weighted training to mitigate dataset imbalance. We benchmarked a diverse range of ML models from classic to the recent Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a transformer-based foundation model designed for small datasets and their ensembles. Performance was validated using nested 10-fold cross-validation and a held-out test set (N = 158). Model interpretability was achieved through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) methods. Results: A stacked ensemble with a LightGBM meta-learner achieved an AUC of 0.9713 (95% CI: 0.9485-0.9874), accuracy of 0.8931 (95% CI: 0.8418-0.9367), and F1-score of 0.8992 (95% CI: 0.8490-0.9420) on the test set. Sensitivity for the high-risk class was 0.946 (35/37). TabPFN showed similar discrimination (AUC: 0.9739). SHAP and LIME analyses identified blood sugar and systolic blood pressure as major contributors to predicted risk. Conclusions: Within this dataset, interpretable ML models achieved high-sensitivity maternal risk stratification using routine clinical data by offering a robust foundation for clinical decision support in low-resource settings, though future research must focus on prospective validation.

title: Dollar Hegemony as International Law-making Power

detail.title: Dollar Hegemony as International Law-making Power
detail.abstract: The so-called weaponisation of the dollar as part of the escalating geopolitical competition has drawn attention to dollar hegemony within the fields of international law, international relations and political economy alike. This article contributes to discussions about the advantages conferred to the US due to the international role of the dollar and to emerging debates about international law and political economy by demonstrating that dollar hegemony operates as a form of international law-making power. The international role of the dollar gives the United States exceptional opportunities not enjoyed by other states to influence disproportionately crucial areas of international law, including the law of jurisdiction and the law of sovereign state immunity. This law-making power has been exercised in contradictory ways. On the one hand, the United States has used the privileged role of the dollar to formulate laws that materially benefited financial capital while also incorporating its logic and ideology. On the other, the United Stated has used the law-making powers of the dollar in order to pursue short-term particularistic, geopolitical and even partisan agendas. Otherwise put, the lawmaking functions of the dollar have reflected-without being able to resolve-the fundamental tensions that arise out of the use of a national currency as world money and, in legal terms, the contradictions that inhere in the fact that a globalized political economy remains mediated by domestic legal and political forms.

title: Plurilateral Trade Agreements: A Complementary Margin to Preferential Liberalization
affiliations: International School of Economics at Tbilisi State University,  and Bielefeld University

detail.title: Plurilateral Trade Agreements: A Complementary Margin to Preferential Liberalization
detail.abstract: We show that plurilateral agreements facilitate global tariff liberalization by creating an MFN-based margin of cooperation that leaves preferential access via preferential trade agreements (PTAs) unchanged. In a model of endogenous trade agreement formation with farsighted governments, PTAs become rigid once exclusion or free-riding incentives bind, constraining further PTA expansion. Plurilateral agreements relax these constraints by allowing countries to liberalize selectively in a differentiated-goods sector without altering existing PTAs. As a result, the stable equilibrium trade network consists of the PTAs that would arise absent plurilaterals, augmented---but not replaced---by plurilateral MFN liberalization. This mechanism provides an explanation for the growing role of sectoral plurilateral agreements within the WTO as preferential liberalization becomes increasingly constrained.

title: Hard Law, Soft Markets: The Heterogeneous Response of Fossil Fuel Equities to Transition Risk News
affiliations: Universidad San Sebastian and Universidad de Talca, Chile

detail.title: Hard Law, Soft Markets: The Heterogeneous Response of Fossil Fuel Equities to Transition Risk News
detail.abstract: Has climate transition risk become priced into fossil fuel equities? We document that market sensitivity to climate news evolved from zero to economically significant over 2007–2023. Using smooth-transition local projections on 598 fossil fuel firms traded on U.S. stock exchanges, we find that unexpected climate media shocks generated no price response before 2014 but produced cumulative 30-day declines of 49 basis points by 2023. This evolution occurred gradually over 2014-2019, consistent with markets progressively updating beliefs about policy credibility rather than reacting to discrete events. Decomposing by news theme reveals striking heterogeneity: enforceable mechanisms like climate legislation (-79 bp) and carbon taxation (-69 bp) trigger substantially stronger responses than voluntary carbon credit markets (-29 bp). These time-varying sensitivities imply static climate betas mismeasure transition exposure, with direct consequences for portfolio risk management, corporate cost-of-capital forecasting, and design of market-credible climate policy.

detail.abstract: The elasticity of taxable income (ETI) parameter is a key quantity in empirical analysis of tax policy and labor supply. We examine when a commonly applied class of ETI estimands can be used to learn about individuals' ETI parameters and their (un)compensated elasticities of labor supply. We begin by providing necessary and sufficient conditions for these estimands to be given a causal interpretation as a positively weighted average of heterogeneous ETI parameters. We then apply these results to empirically analyze a reform of the Norwegian tax system that reduced the marginal tax rates on middle and high incomes. The estimated ETI parameters increase steadily with income, meaning high-income individuals are more responsive to tax changes than middle-income individuals. Next, we show how (un)compensated elasticities of labor supply can be bounded directly from the ETI estimands, or point identified by combining these estimands with estimates of earnings responses to lottery winnings. The results suggest an (un)compensated elasticity of 0.1 (0.0) for middle-income individuals. The (un)compensated elasticity estimates increase steadily with income to around 0.45 (0.3) for high-income individuals. These findings imply a substantial excess burden of taxation, and that reducing top-income tax rates would increase tax revenue. Our findings are also informative about how the intertemporal elasticity of substitution and the Frisch elasticity vary across the income distribution.

title: Societal Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence Support in Legal Representation: A Survey-Based Evaluation
affiliations: Independent and Independent

detail.title: Societal Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence Support in Legal Representation: A Survey-Based Evaluation
detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into legal services has generated significant debate regarding trust, accountability, fairness, and ethical responsibility. This study examines public perception of AI-assisted legal representation through a survey-based analysis conducted with 146 participants. The research explores attitudes toward the use of artificial intelligence across different stages of legal processes, ranging from supportive and low-risk functions through decision-influencing applications. The findings revealed a notably divided pulic opinion, with attitudes often approaching and even balanced between accaptance and skepticism. However, despite this apparent equilibrium, the results indicate that positive perceptions towards AI-assisted legal services are comparatively strong given the novelty of articial intelligence in the legal domain. The emergency of such a level of public trust at an early stage of technological integration suggests a rapid shift in societal attitudes toward AI-supported legal practice. Acceptance increases significantly when artifical intelligence is framed as a supportive tool operating under human oversight, while concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, accountability, and the absence of human judgment continue to shape public hesitation. Beyond measuring public attitudes, the study aims to provide guidance for legal professionals by identifying societal trust thresholds and expectations surrounding AI use in legal representation. In this regard, the findings offer and informative framework for lawyers seeking to integrate artificial intelligence into their professional activities while maintaining ethical standards, transparency, and public confidence.

detail.abstract: As climate shocks intensify, it is increasingly important to understand how investors adapt to physical climate risk. This paper examines how institutional investors adjust their commercial real estate (CRE) portfolios after experiencing localized extreme heat near their headquarters. We use a novel dataset that links United States (US) CRE transactions to property-level climate risk and apply a stacked difference-indifferences design to isolate changes in investment behavior. After heat shocks, investors acquire properties with 7.4% lower expected climate losses and sell assets with 4.8% higher losses. These two-sided adjustments persist for up to four years and are driven mainly by financial institutions and private funds. Public REITs and pension funds show no significant response. Despite these shifts, we find no evidence of climate risk discounts in transaction prices. Treated investors also increase capital spending on building improvements and insurance, suggesting complementary efforts to reduce portfolio exposure.

detail.abstract: This educational paper synthesizes contemporary evidence on dance-based physical activity, hypertension management, cardiometabolic risk reduction, and belly-dance-specific practice in order to provide a safe and academically grounded teaching resource for community programs serving adult women. The paper does not argue that belly dance is a stand-alone treatment for hypertension or cardiometabolic disease. Instead, it positions adapted belly dance as a culturally meaningful, low-impact, adherence-friendly movement modality that can plausibly support physical activity participation, functional conditioning, psychosocial wellbeing, and selected risk-factor management when designed within clear safety parameters. The evidence base is mixed but promising: meta-analyses of dance interventions in adults with hypertension report reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, broader exercise literature consistently supports moderate-intensity activity for blood-pressure control, and belly-dance-specific studies suggest benefits for quality of life, self-image, fatigue, pain, and function in selected populations. Building from this literature and from practice-based instructional logic, the paper proposes a teaching framework for blood-pressure-conscious community instruction. Key components include participant triage, red-flag screening, intensity scaling, breath-aware cueing, movement classification by cardiovascular and postural demand, safe progression across a 12-week curriculum, and practical documentation procedures for instructors running non-clinical programs. The paper also distinguishes between appropriate educational claims and claims that should remain within the scope of clinical research. Its purpose is to help educators, program coordinators, and community leaders build responsible belly dance classes for adults with sedentary lifestyles, elevated cardiometabolic risk, or a desire for enjoyable, sustainable, nonintimidating physical activity. In doing so, it contributes an applied educational framework that translates dispersed literature into a coherent resource for program design, teaching practice, and future scholarly development.

detail.abstract: The tendency for children of self-employed to follow in their parents' footsteps is well-documented, but less is known about the mechanisms underlying this correlation: inheritance of a family business or wealth, direct learning-by-doing, or more general skills and preferences passed across generations. In this paper, we examine micro-data from seven countries (Hungary, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Russia, and China) that experienced decades of central planning during which private business ownership was prohibited, and therefore the financial and direct learning channels for intergenerational transmission were largely eliminated. Despite a gap of at least 40 years under a different economic system and in most cases a skipping of generations, we find that entrepreneurship (measured as self-employment, employer business ownership, or employer with five or more employees) increases by more than 50 percent among individuals whose parents or grandfathers owned businesses just prior to the communist takeovers. The strength of intergenerational links from pre-to post-communism are only slightly lower than parent-child entrepreneurship links in the U.S. These results support important roles for the general human capital and preferences channels, either through genetics or informal inculcation of skills and attitudes. Countries experiencing relatively relaxed communist regimes display a stronger correlation, possibly because of more possibilities for informal transmission. Family business background is associated with positive attitudes towards risk-taking, and higher earnings among employees, but no greater premium among self-employed. Maternal grandfathers influence entrepreneurship and risk-taking attitudes more than paternal grandfathers, which is consistent with a "kitchen table" transmission mechanism. “Small production engenders capitalism and the bourgeoisie continuously, daily, hourly, spontaneously, and on a mass scale.” – Vladimir Ilyich Lenin, “Left-Wing Communism, an Infantile Disorder,” 1920

detail.title: Does Scarcity Tax Parents' Minds?

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-46

detail.abstract: Parents with limited income spend less time than their advantaged counterparts engaging in educational activities with their children. A common explanation is that financial scarcity creates a "bandwidth tax" on cognition. The scarcity framework highlights two components: attentional capacity (the ability to focus amid competing demands) and executive control (the ability to resist temptation and act in line with long-term goals). No study has tested which is the primary constraint on parental investment or separated subjective financial stress from income itself. We address both gaps through the Early Investment Project, a survey of 1,932 mothers of kindergartners in Chicago Public Schools that simultaneously measures felt scarcity, household income, attentional capacity, and present bias. Our outcome captures parent-reported obstacles to fulfilling intentions to read with their child. Two main findings emerge. First, attentional capacity-not self-control-is the primary constraint: the Attention Index is associated with all four parent-side barriers at the 1% level across all models, including those with strict controls for depression, agency, and growth mindset, while present bias is essentially uncorrelated with the outcomes. Second, felt scarcity, not household income, is associated with attentional deficits: the scarcity coefficient on the Attention Index persists when income is controlled, whereas income shows no independent association with attention. Placebo tests confirm specificity. These results indicate that attention, not self-control, is the mechanism through which financial insecurity is linked to reduced parental investment, and that perceived insufficiency, rather than income, is its primary correlate.

title: Who Benefits from Higher-Education Expansion? Rank-Based Inequality and Opportunity in India

detail.title: Who Benefits from Higher-Education Expansion? Rank-Based Inequality and Opportunity in India
detail.abstract: This paper provides a distributionally grounded assessment of higher-education access in India. It moves beyond aggregate participation rates and group-level gaps to quantify rank-dependent inequality and its mediation through state-level fee-waiver regimes. Drawing on nationally representative Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) 2023-24 data, we estimate Erreygers-normalized concentration indices for household level higher-education enrolment (national ECI =-0.106, indicating pronounced pro-rich skew comparable to stratified international systems) and fee-waiver receipt, complemented by exact decompositions into circumstance contributions and state-level benefit-incidence gradients. A novel decomposition attributes virtually all observed inequality to predetermined factors-household size dominates (153% contribution via poverty-linked resource dilution), partially offset by parental (especially maternal) education-yielding lower-bound inequality-of-opportunity estimates that expose stratified massification beneath rising totals. Subnationally, stark heterogeneity emerges: northern laggards like Bihar (-0.134) and Delhi (-0.251) sustain steep pro-rich gradients, while southern states show milder bias; fee waivers function as "targeted gateways" in pro-poor settings (e.g., Arunachal Pradesh,-0.121 waiver ECI with high beneficiary uptake) but as "untargeted expansions" elsewhere (e.g., Andhra Pradesh's 61% participation yet neutral incidence). Bivariate regimes highlight how high access coexists with regressive targeting, or progressive design falters without enrollment gains, underscoring that expansion has reinforced circumstance-driven barriers distorting talent allocation. Policy must pivot from volume targets to equity-focused reforms addressing upstream constraints like fertility-poverty traps.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Blockchain First-Principles Analysis (BFPA) framework, a novel methodology for the epistemic evaluation of distributed ledger systems. Unlike conventional blockchain assessment approaches that rely on performance metrics, tokenomics, or decentralization indices, BFPA constructs a rigorous derivation chain from physical laws and cryptographic assumptions through an action axiom to concrete protocol design decisions. The framework systematically identifies structural failure points by testing whether each design choice is derivable from foundational axioms or represents an ad hoc decision vulnerable to obsolescence.

The framework introduces several analytical innovations: (i) a four-level axiom hierarchy anchoring evaluation in physics, cryptography, praxeology, and social consensus; (ii) a Nash equilibrium gate mechanism for social layer stability; (iii) a four-stage stability profile progressing from Nash equilibrium through evolutionarily stable strategies and lock-in to self-referential feedback; (iv) a lock-in typology distinguishing design-emergent, ecosystem-emergent, corporate-imposed, and regulatory-granted lock-in; and (v) a network effect genesis model identifying five necessary conditions for spontaneous adoption without marketing.

We apply the framework systematically to eight major blockchain systems: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Monero, XRP, Polkadot, Tezos, and BNB Chain. The analysis reveals that epistemic design quality alone correlates weakly with market price and adoption. Lock-in type and network effect genesis conditions are substantially stronger predictors. This finding provides a principled explanation for two empirical puzzles: the Tezos Paradox (superior governance design, declining price) and the Monero Paradox (strong epistemic foundations, stagnant adoption). The framework provides a falsifiable, non-speculative methodology for institutional evaluation of blockchain systems as coordination mechanisms.

title: Gender Diversity Improves Performance but Reinforces Gendered Roles
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Gender Diversity Improves Performance but Reinforces Gendered Roles
detail.abstract: Does group gender diversity benefit individuals? I examine this question with a field experiment randomizing 3,060 students to small study groups at university entry. Assignment to mixed-gender rather than single-gender groups improves performance and well-being for both men and women: first-year grades increase by about 0.10 SD, well-being by 0.15 SD, and program dropout falls by 6 pp (24%). However, mixed-gender groups also induce more traditional attitudes toward family gender roles. Mechanism analyses suggest that gender diversity fosters collaboration and shifts gender attitudes by reinforcing gendered roles in social interaction: while women coordinate and ask questions, men compete and explain.

detail.title: Climate Change, Macroeconomic Factors and the Nigerian Indigenous Meat and Milk Industry: A Long-Memory Approach

keywords: Nigerian indigenous milk and meat production

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between climate change, macroeconomic variables and indigenous livestock production in Nigeria over the period 1981–2023 using fractional integration and multivariate regression methods. More specifically, it examines how temperature and precipitation anomalies, including their nonlinear (squared) effects, agricultural conditions and macroeconomic factors affect Total Indigenous Livestock Meat (TOLIM), Raw Milk of Cattle (RAMOC), and the combined value of Meat and Milk (TOVOMAMI). Climate variables enter the models in levels, while the other variables are first-differenced and log-transformed where appropriate, to ensure stationarity and balanced regressions. The specifications assuming white noise residuals suggest weak and largely statistically insignificant effects of the climate variables on livestock productivity, and also yield some slight evidence of an impact of macroeconomic factors. By contrast, when imposing an AR(1) specification on the error term, negative effects of permanent pasture and exchange rate depreciation on output values are found. These results suggest possible inefficiencies in land use and macroeconomic vulnerability in Nigeria’s indigenous livestock sector. and provide useful information for designing sustainable livestock adaptation policies in low-income economies.
